record.paper_title: Open questions on the impact of an inflated ball
record.context_brief: Global inflated-ball impact model and dissipation mechanism
record.original_question: For inflated sports balls impacting a rigid surface, what predictive model can determine the contact time, coefficient of restitution, and impact-energy loss as functions of inflation pressure, initial impact velocity, and shell mechanical properties? Such a model should account for the coupled deformation of the shell and compression of the internal gas, and it should identify the physical dissipation mechanism that controls the restitution coefficient rather than leaving competing explanations such as momentum-flux dissipation, shell vibrations, gas dissipation, and solid friction unresolved.

evidence.quote: Despite a good understanding of ball elasticity, the source of energy dissipation for inflated balls remains controversial. We first give a clear view of non-dissipative impact mechanics. Second we review, analyse and estimate the different sources of energy dissipation of the multi-physics phenomena that occur during the impact. Finally, we propose several experiments to decide between gas compression, shell visco-elastic dissipation, solid friction, sound emission or shell vibrations as the major source of energy dissipation.
The goal of this paper is to investigate the mechanics of inflated balls. More precisely, how does impact characteristics depend onto inflation pressure, impact velocities and shell properties?

However, the source of dissipation is still unclear and several authors have given various explanations to stand for it such as momentum flux force dissipation (Stronge & Ashcroft 2007), vibrations of the shell (Cross 2014), dissipation in the gas (Georgallas & Landry 2015) and solid friction (Pauchard & Rica 1998). No consensus arose to answer this question, especially no model gives the dependency of ball dissipation coefficient (or similarly coefficient of restitution) on inflation pressure.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider an inflated, thin-shelled ball (e.g., a sports ball) with internal gauge pressure P, shell of thickness h made of a material with given mechanical properties (Young's modulus E, Poisson ratio ν, and viscoelastic loss characteristics), radius R, and total mass m. The ball impacts normally a rigid, flat, stationary surface with initial velocity v₀, undergoes finite deformation of the shell coupled with adiabatic/isothermal compression of the enclosed gas, and rebounds with velocity v₁.

Develop a predictive mechanical model for the impact that:

1. Treats the coupled dynamics of shell deformation and the compression of the internal gas during contact.
2. Predicts the contact time τ(P, v₀, shell properties), the coefficient of restitution e = v₁/v₀ as a function of (P, v₀, shell properties), and the fraction of kinetic energy ΔE/E₀ dissipated during impact.
3. Identifies, among the candidate dissipation mechanisms — (a) momentum-flux force at the contact patch, (b) elastic vibrations of the shell, (c) thermodynamic/viscous dissipation in the enclosed gas, (d) viscoelastic dissipation in the shell material, and (e) acoustic radiation / solid friction — the dominant physical mechanism that controls e as a function of inflation pressure, and quantitatively reproduces experimentally observed dependencies (in particular, the empirical increase of e with P toward a saturation value, and the decrease of e with v₀).

Provide closed-form or reduced-order expressions for τ, e, and ΔE/E₀ in terms of the dimensionless groups built from P, v₀, R, m, h, and the shell moduli, and resolve which single mechanism is dominant rather than leaving multiple competing explanations unranked.
artifact.status_search_result: Partial mechanistic models exist (e.g., Georgallas & Landry 2016 derive a formula for the coefficient of restitution as a function of gauge pressure and shell shear modulus, validated against experiments above ~25 kPa), and several competing dissipation mechanisms have been proposed (momentum-flux force, shell vibrations, gas dissipation, viscoelastic shell losses, solid friction). However, no single consensus model identifies the dominant dissipation mechanism across the full relevant range of pressures and impact velocities, so the problem remains open in the sense of selecting and validating a unifying mechanism.

status_evidence.title: The coefficient of restitution of pressurized balls: a mechanistic model
status_evidence.snippet: Mechanistic model giving the coefficient of restitution as a function of gauge pressure and shell shear modulus, fitting experimental data well above 25 kPa.
status_evidence.claim: A partial mechanistic model exists relating e to inflation pressure and shell properties, but it does not definitively settle the dominant dissipation mechanism.

status_evidence.title: Open questions on the impact of an inflated ball (Request PDF)
status_evidence.snippet: Reviews competing explanations — momentum-flux dissipation, shell vibrations, gas dissipation, solid friction — and notes no consensus on the dominant mechanism.
status_evidence.claim: The identification of the dominant dissipation mechanism remains controversial in the literature.

status_evidence.title: Air Pressure and the Coefficient of Restitution of a Ball
status_evidence.snippet: Empirical study showing e increases with pressure and decreases with impact speed, with exponential relationship to pressure.
status_evidence.claim: Empirical phenomenology is documented, but a complete predictive model selecting one mechanism is not established.
